articles.title: Java4Shell: RCE in OpenJDK when processing Base64
articles.content: The Tail of Base64 By Quang Luong On affected OpenJDK builds, malformed Base64 data can cause a constant-value overwrite of allocated heap memory. Through remote Heap Feng Shui, we turn that overwrite into a heap leak and remote code execution. Discovery A few months back, I was developing a 0-click exploit on a certain phone vendor. The bug was constrained: it is a linear out-of-bounds write and we have no way to bypass ASLR. I almost considered it unexploitable until I audited the Android Runtime. Turns out, it has some predictable memory allocation pattern and if you align the registers from the starting memory corruption just right you can make the runtime interpret attacker's bytecode. Lesson learned Complicated system interactions are hard, and this complexity can make exploiting hard bugs easy. After completing that exploit chain, inspired (and bored), I decided to look into some thing completely different. So I pulled the official JVM implementation (OpenJDK HotSpot) and started auditing. Java is a mature platform, so I was aware that having a "good" bug here would be hard, but I wanted to give it my best attempt anyway. Recalling my earlier lesson that complex systems and code crossing multiple boundaries are difficult to get right, I focused the audit on the JIT compiler, intrinsics, widely accessible APIs, and cryptography. Well, more precisely, I told Codex to look at those areas like any serious security researcher in 2026. To be honest, I didn't expect to find anything trivially exploitable, perhaps only some logic flaws or side-channel issues. Most early results Codex brought me were slops, either unreachable or the requirement of exploitation is not realistic at all. This looks like a gamble I am going to lose. But you know what, fortune favors the bold. So I just prompted harder... Eventually, Codex brought me a finding for a memory corruption in the Base64 decoder itself. I came looking for copper and found gold, through sheer persistence. But wait, is it really gold, or just fool's gold? Note That sheer persistence is prompting AI and ignoring slops for around 20 minutes, by the way. The vulnerability The issue lies in OpenJDK HotSpot's x86-64 Base64 intrinsic. C2 is the most aggressive JIT compiler in the Java Virtual Machine. Specifically, if you trigger a function repeatedly, then it will compile that function into native code. Even then, ordinary native code itself is not fast enough. Modern CPUs have specialized instructions that allow processing data even faster. HotSpot uses them in optimized routines called intrinsics. The x86-64 Base64 intrinsic miscalculated the padded tail's store mask, causing an out-of-bounds write. The x86-64 Base64 intrinsic iterates through the input in 256-byte blocks; if it is less than 256, then it will do so in 64-byte blocks. When the input is less than 64 bytes, it uses evmovdqub , the intrinsic for the VMOVDQU8 instruction. This instruction takes a 64-bit mask that decides which bytes are
articles.summary: 研究者披露 Java4Shell 漏洞：OpenJDK 处理畸形 Base64 数据可致堆内存覆写，进而实现远程代码执行。

articles.title: Highly classified US national security communications network goes down
articles.content: The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter. The NSA closed its campus to most employees on Tuesday night, reverting to essential personnel only as it works to restore the network, according to a voicemail inbox used by NSA employees and a source familiar with the matter. The move to further restrict staffing levels came just hours after the NSA told employees they could return to work as normal. It is not clear what prompted the reversal. The agency had staggered employee arrivals earlier in the day as it worked to address the issue. The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said. “The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.” A source familiar with the matter told CNN that restoration of the network was ongoing but not yet complete. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said later Tuesday afternoon that the NSA outage was the result of the agency applying a software patch to address major software vulnerabilities that were discovered last month. “The patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected,” Clayton said on Fox Business. “That is that is what has happened at the NSA today.” The vulnerabilities Clayton were referring to are in PHP, a programming language that powers about 70% of the world’s websites. AI tools helped researchers exploit them, setting off a scramble by government agencies and corporations around the world to address the issue in recent weeks. The NSA itself urged organizations to apply software patches. The flaws in PHP could allow hackers to break into websites and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords. Clayton said there is no sign that any of the recent tech outages, including that affecting the NSA, were the result of a cyberattack. A current and a former US official said an outage at NSANet would not impact the agency’s ability to communicate urgent intelligence to President Donald Trump while he is traveling in Asia on Air Force One. Both sources described multiple redundancies and backup networks that the government could use to communicate securely with the president who is currently in the Philippines before heading to China tomorrow for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. NSANet is “more of a network of networks, and it’s unlikely that a f

We published our anniversary launch release in print at Defcon 33, HOPE, WHY25 and some additional variations at several conferences around the world including AlligatorCon, B-Sides Canberra, Out of the Box, Datenspuren, DistrictCon, OffensiveCon, Recon, and Toorcamp. We included a CTF with exploit challenges and had puzzles and easter eggs included in the zine. We threw parties and had talks at Defcon and WHY25 to celebrate this milestone. More importantly, we got new research into people's hands. The point of the relaunch was to get people reading, researching, writing, and contributing again. We wanted the next person picking up Phrack to find something that made them sit down at a computer and start pulling a system apart. We owe a huge thanks to the authors, editors, artists, publishing partners, donors, and staff who made it happen. Writing the paper, working through revisions, putting the print editions together, paying the bills, and getting boxes of zines to the right places all take time and effort. Most of that work is invisible when you are holding the finished issue. We appreciate everyone who did it. And to the readers: thank you for giving a shit. Seeing someone get excited about an article, connect it to something they are working on, or realize that they could contribute something themselves makes the effort worthwhile. That exchange is how this thing keeps going. The relaunch worked, and this issue is the follow-through. This is the third release curated by the new staff, and we are not slowing down. This issue is larger than last year's, with 23 main papers and eight additional articles in Line Noise. There is also work examining backdoors in machine learning and what it means to trust an AI system. articles.title: Google's AI answers reducing search traffic by 40%
articles.content: Google's AI answers are taking clicks from websites in the search results. In a randomized experiment, researchers hid AI Overviews from some US desktop users. Comparing them with users who still saw Overviews shows that an Overview cuts clicks to outside websites by about 40%. Those Overviews now appear on more than half the US keywords DataForSEO tracks, up from 6% two years ago. The industry's answer, GEO (generative engine optimization), has yet to show a way to compensate for the loss. While AI citations correlate with the same kind of link profile that goes with higher Google rankings, in March AI assistants sent websites just 0.3% of their traffic. Search engine optimization (SEO) still decides whether you can be found, but where an AI answer appears, a ranking brings 40% fewer visits than it used to. Generative engine optimization (GEO), the practice of getting your content cited in AI-written answers, looks mostly like SEO plus two additions: being present on the third-party sites AI answers draw from, and writing pages that are easy to quote. We found little evidence for any other tactic. Google answers first An AI Overview is a generated summary that Google places above the ordinary results, with links to the pages it drew on. In DataForSEO's monthly panel of 20 million keywords, the share of results showing one climbed from 5.93% in September 2024 to 61.43% in August 2026. The chart at the top of this post shows that climb. Over the same period the featured snippet, the quoted passage Google used to show at the top of a page, fell from 8.96% to 0.44%, and the discussions and forums block fell from 21.13% to 7.42%. Video results rose from 9.67% to 19.98%, though that is down from a peak of 31.05% in October 2025, and local map listings rose from 19.98% to 25.99%. DataForSEO's dataset covers 190 million keywords, 165 million AI answers, and 1.1 billion backlinks, mostly for US English searches. Pew Research Center's data gives an independent check. Pew logged the searches of 900 US adults in March 2025, re-ran them in April, and found summaries on 18% of them. DataForSEO's figures for those months are 14.67% and 17.63%, close to Pew's. You can't reliably avoid Overviews by choosing different keywords. Between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the third quarter of 2026, the rate rose for every type of search intent: Search intent Q4 2025 Q3 2026 Informational (looking something up) 48.42% 70.44% Commercial (comparing options) 26.30% 51.35% Navigational (looking for a site) 17.04% 34.03% Transactional (ready to buy) 10.82% 28.64% Low-volume keywords aren't safer either. In the third quarter of 2026, keywords with 201 to 300 monthly searches showed Overviews 58.59% of the time, against 48.62% for those above 600. A separate dataset, from June to September 2026, covers difficulty and price. The easiest keywords showed Overviews 60.64% of the time and the hardest 53.76%. articles.title: Quad9's withdrawal from France: A canary in the coal mine
articles.content: Last month, the Swiss non-profit foundation Quad9 announced that it will withdraw its free public DNS resolver from France. This difficult decision followed months of litigation and a French court ruling that imposed daily financial penalties on Quad9 for failing to block domains associated with alleged copyright infringement. Quad9’s departure from France is both disheartening and understandable. The court’s ruling put the organization in the impossible bind of having to choose between crippling litigation and penalties, or fundamentally altering its service in a way that would undermine the privacy and security of its users. Left with no good option, Quad9 is choosing the exit door instead. The withdrawal of a basic infrastructure service from France fundamentally harms the free and open Internet, and it should serve as a warning of the damage that will result if rightsholders and policymakers continue demanding maximal blocking across every layer of the Internet. It not only deprives French Internet users of a trustworthy and important tool; it creates a real risk of disruption to their daily lives. Quad9’s resolver is used by a wide variety of individuals and organizations in France — including government bodies, educational institutions, hospitals, and utilities — and Quad9 has no way to directly notify those individuals and institutions that their resolver will soon stop working. If the affected parties do not change their resolver before Quad9 removes its service, their Internet will fail with no explanation. Quad9 is not the first public DNS resolver to withdraw from a country following blocking orders, and it almost certainly won’t be the last. Cisco previously withdrew its OpenDNS resolver from France, Portugal, and Belgium (temporarily) under similar circumstances. And a Belgian court recently issued an order that would impose substantial penalties if Cloudflare, Google, and Cisco do not begin blocking websites through their public resolvers by early January 2027. That’s something Cloudflare has never done. Cloudflare has spent years advocating against orders of this kind. We are concerned that rightsholders’ unrelenting demands for blocking by public DNS resolvers will end up causing real harm to the Internet. A refresher on DNS, the Domain Name System To understand why this is such a problem, it helps to understand how the Internet works under the hood. DNS resolvers are a foundational piece of the Internet’s infrastructure. DNS is the Internet’s address book: when you type a website name such as cloudflare.com, the DNS system translates that domain name into the IP address your device needs to connect to it. A DNS resolver is the service that looks up that address and sends it back to your device, much like an operator finding a phone number in a directory. DNS resolvers can be operated by anyone, but they are commonly run by Internet service providers (ISPs), mobile networks, businesses, and universities. If you’re reading this blo

articles.title: Actual curl rewrites in rust
articles.content: For a long time we have received repeated requests for, or questions about, a curl rewrite in rust. Often as a joke, but also seriously. A joke from years ago In this modern world of AIs, we have only been waiting for someone to prove it possible and now it seems we don’t have to wait anymore. This fall seems to be the time of the curl-in-rust takes as we first saw urlx appear a few months ago, claimed to be a memory-safe, from-scratch reimplementation of curl and libcurl and now in November curl, rewritten in Rust – a rewrite of curl and libcurl in Rust . This second one confusingly enough not even using a different name. This latter one claims to have spent 8,600 USD to make it happen. Writing code once was never the issue Writing code once was never the big deal with software and it still isn’t. Sure, it’s fascinating that you can make a set of agents accomplish this in only a few weeks but let’s face it: it could do this because all the AIs of the world have trained on curl code for years. curl is extremely well documented, there are hundreds of existing open source application using its API and there are thousands of test cases to verify the implementation. The C code sits there and all the AI needs to do is convert it to rust, then polish until the tests work. A know-it-all person’s comment from years ago curl is the result of time curl has come to be what it is thanks to many decisions, lots of time, many users, oceans of feedback and many iterations. Sure, recreating what curl is at any specific single moment in time is certainly doable. Doable, because we have made a perfect specification for that project. Behind already During the time these agents converted 185,000 lines of C code into 340,000 lines of Rust code (I counted), we merged over 300 commits in the actual curl project. We actually improved curl during these a little more than three weeks. A little over 200 bugfixes actually. 200 bugfixes that none of those rust rewrites have. We also fixed a few vulnerabilities. In another month we have done another 200 and maybe fixed a few more vulnerabilities. Will these clones keep up? The constant tweaking, fixing, improving and extending is what makes a software project live, what makes it attractive to users and what makes it able to compete with alternatives. That fixing, and occasional new feature, is a direct result of a working community of users, contributors and maintainers. That goes way beyond the source code or which language that is used. A primary reason it is hard to make a competing curl alternative is because of the development speed, the development team and the community around curl. It is not because of the chosen language it is implemented in. Only curl can boast decades of ABI and API stability and prove that we know this and can do it well – over time. An alternative that pops up today might be able to do it as well, and in a few decades we will know if they could . C I know I’m repeating myself but: out of the 81 v

articles.title: Redict is deprecated
articles.content: November 17, 2026 I must unfortunately announce that Redict is officially deprecated, and Redict 7.3.6 is the final release. I had hoped to rally the Redis diaspora around a copyleft initiative, to protect ourselves from future rug-pulls, and made Redict to serve this purpose. However, with the valkey project’s success, and Redis’s return to a copyleft license, Redict was not able to build a sustainable community. We recommend that Redict users switch to valkey , which uses a permissive license but has better long-term prospects. We advise against switching back to Redis; though it is once again open source, and copyleft, it uses a contributor license agreement which will facilitate another rug-pull when Redis has a bad financial quarter. Switching to valkey is straightforward: if you install from your package manager, simply install valkey and move your config file: # mv /etc/redict.conf /etc/valkey.conf If you use containers, simply pull the valkey container instead and ensure that it runs with the appropriate config file. Thanks to everyone who has contributed to Redict, endorsed the fork as the future of Redis, and switched to it on their own machines. We had a good run :)
articles.summary: Redis 分支项目 Redict 宣布弃用，7.3.6 为最终版本，作者称未能凝聚社区形成 copyleft 替代方案。

articles.title: How Rust Changed Me As A Developer
articles.content: How Rust Changed Me As A Developer The programming language you use affects how you think as a software developer . That may seem surprising to you; you may have picked up JavaScript pretty quickly knowing Python, and it didn't really affect how you think or develop. That's because those languages are pretty similar. The more different a programming language is from what you're used to, the more it can change you. Rust was quite different to me, so it did. I've been developing with Rust for over 6 years; more than 4 years professionally now . One of the reasons I really wanted to become more proficient with Rust is because I knew it would challenge me, and hopefully change me for the better as a developer. I think it did. What I learned and am going to discuss here is not exclusive to Rust. You can encounter many of these concepts in other contexts, and indeed I had encountered quite a few of them already. But in this case, Rust helped bring them into better focus. Where were enums all my life? We're all familiar with product types, though not usually under that name: struct Human { first_name : String, last_name : String, } The fields of the Human struct can vary independently from each other, and we have to deal with all possible combinations: all possible first names and last names, combined. The product of their combinations, to to speak. But it turns out there's another type thing that's been around forever but that the programming community has mostly been been ignoring : the sum type. A sum type expresses variants: something is either one thing, or another, out of a bunch of variants: enum Person { Human { first_name: String , last_name: String }, Cat { name: String , cuteness: Cuteness } } A Person is either a human or a cat: that's the sum of the possiblities. Each variant can have data associated with it, and this can be a product type, but the Person type is just these options (two in this case). In code where you need to deal with a person, you need to handle each variant by match in on the object. The Rust compiler enforces this. match some_person { Human { first_name, last_name } => { // do a thing with first_name and last_name }, Cat { name, cuteness } => { // do a thing with name and cutenes } } When you handle the human variant, you only need to worry about first_name and last_name . You don't have to worry about name or cuteness at all. These cases are distinct from each other. It turns out that it's really helpful to model stuff using sum types. People using functional programming languages already knew this. You can model optionality ( null ) this way: you got either some value, or nothing. You can also model errors: it's either okay (with whatever value you return in case of success), or an error (with a value describing the error). Any language without sum types now feels impoverished to me. I know I can simulate it with some type field, but the job of a programming language is to help me handle basic stuff, and this is basi

Perhaps the biggest hurdle was getting over the process to assign copyright to the Free Software Foundation , which does feel a bit archaic (download, sign, and return a PDF) and slow (mostly waiting for an email response), though hey, I have nothing but sympathy. Open source is unsustainably tricky. As consumers, we often like free as in freedom and free as in beer, but neither pay the bills. We hope some company steps in to fund these projects, but that rarely happens. As a result, most open source projects are starved (even popular ones), run by volunteers working for free. All that is to say, if the upstream Emacs contribution/onboarding process seems less than ideal, cut it some slack. The project as a whole primarily runs on the blood, sweat, and tears of unpaid contributors. If you can, fund the maintainers you rely on (or better yet, get your employer to do so). If you've been thinking of contributing to Emacs upstream, don't procrastinate like me and just give it a try. Compared to the typical GitHub pull-request process, your first Emacs contribution may feel a little daunting and dated, but there's a lovely fuzzy light at the end of the tunnel. You see, Emacs has been around for 50 years . Very few software projects get to live this long. Landing contributions on a project with such a rich history is a real treat! But I digress… Let's get moving. Once I got over procrastinating, I finally got a handful of small contributions landed on the master branch. Thank you, Eli Zaretskii, Stefan Kangas, and Gerd Möllmann, for your help. From then on, I eagerly waited for them to formally make it to a stable release. Emacs 31 shipped the lot. Hide Dired's absolute location I do enjoy a visual (and functional) tweak here and there , and a Dired tweak felt small enough to be the perfect candidate for my very first Emacs contribution. With that in mind, I tweaked dired-hide-details-mode by adding the dired-hide-details-hide-absolute-location user option, which hides the directory's absolute path, typically displayed at the top of Dired buffers ( bug#72272 , commit ). More on this in my Hide another detail post. macOS speech recognition permission At some point, I ran into a snag trying to run macosrec from my beloved eshell . The process just crashed with a cryptic abort trap: 6 , so the issue wasn't super obvious. It turned out the utility required granting an OS permission that can only be requested by the host app (Emacs) if it includes the relevant description in its Info.plist file. articles.title: How to Bypass Rust's Orphan Rule
articles.content: Write Rust for long enough, and you are bound to run into error[E0117] . Take a simple, everyday scenario. You pull in a serialization library that defines a ToJson trait, along with a third-party type library like uuid . You want to turn a uuid::Uuid into JSON, so you naturally write: impl ToJson for uuid :: Uuid { fn to_json ( & self ) -> String { format! ( " \" {} \" " , self ) } } And the compiler immediately stops you: error[E0117]: only traits defined in the current crate can be implemented for types defined outside of the crate This is Rust's well-known Orphan Rule . Once people hit this wall, they usually either complain that the compiler is too rigid or dutifully wrap the type in a NewType. But if you look closely at how the Orphan Rule actually works, it is not a dead end. By design, it leaves a pretty wide door open. What Is the Orphan Rule Actually Protecting Against? Setting the jargon aside, the logic behind the Orphan Rule is simple: if you want a type to implement a trait, at least one of those two things (the type or the trait) must belong to your own crate. In plain English, you don't get to make rules for someone else's types. Suppose crate A implements ToJson for uuid::Uuid and outputs a hyphenated UUID string, while crate B also implements ToJson for uuid::Uuid and outputs 32 raw hex characters without hyphens. If a project depends on both A and B, the compiler has a problem when it sees uuid.to_json() : which implementation should it pick? To prevent this kind of global conflict, Rust enforces coherence , and the Orphan Rule is how it gets enforced. There is nothing wrong with the rule itself. It keeps the Rust ecosystem from turning into a mess as dependency trees grow. The catch is that real-world projects constantly run into a very common need: making a third-party type implement a trait from another third-party crate. Neither the type nor the trait is yours, yet gluing libraries together like this happens all the time. So what can you do? Why the Two Usual Workarounds Fall Short Right now, the Rust ecosystem mostly relies on two workarounds. Both appear to solve the problem on the surface, but because neither addresses the root cause, they get awkward fast. 1. Building it into the library Many foundational crates take this route: since users can't write the impl themselves, the crate provides it internally. Because ToJson is defined inside the crate, implementing it for any external type satisfies the Orphan Rule. Open up the Cargo.toml of one of these crates, and you will see a long list of feature flags: with-uuid , with-chrono , with-time , with-jiff , with-url , with-rust-decimal , and so on. It looks helpful at first, but it tries to enumerate an open, constantly changing ecosystem inside a single crate . That approach has clear limits, and the downsides show up quickly: You can never support everything. Today the community favors chrono , tomorrow people switch to jiff , and next week your team builds its own inter

articles.title: Program-as-Weights: A Programming Paradigm for Fuzzy Functions
articles.content: [Submitted on 2 Jul 2026 ( v1 ), last revised 7 Nov 2026 (this version, v2)] Title: Program-as-Weights: A Programming Paradigm for Fuzzy Functions Authors: Wentao Zhang , Liliana Hotsko , Woojeong Kim , Pengyu Nie , Stuart Shieber , Yuntian Deng View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Many everyday programming tasks resist clean rule-based implementation, such as alerting on important log lines, repairing malformed JSON, or ranking search results by intent, and are increasingly outsourced to large language model APIs at the cost of locality, reproducibility, and price. We propose fuzzy-function programming: compiling such a function from a natural-language specification into a compact, locally executable neural artifact. We instantiate this paradigm with Program-as-Weights (PAW), in which a 4B compiler trained on FuzzyBench, a 10M-example dataset we release, emits parameter-efficient adapters for a frozen, lightweight interpreter. A 0.6B Qwen3 interpreter executing PAW programs matches the performance of direct prompting of Qwen3-32B, while using roughly one fiftieth of the inference memory and running at 30 tokens/s on a MacBook M3. PAW reframes the foundation model from a per-input problem solver into a tool builder: invoked once per function definition, it produces a small reusable artifact whose subsequent calls per function application are cheap and offline.

articles.title: C’s designated initializers give us named arguments
articles.content:
In my previous post I talked about C++’s “relatively nerfed” form of designated initializers. This time I want to show you a neat thing you can do with C’s full-power designated initializers. I first saw this pattern in Ben Klemens’ book 21st Century C (2014), pages 226–228. ( Godbolt. ) struct IdealVolumeArgs { double atm; // P double moles; // n double kelvin; // T }; #define ideal_volume(...) ideal_volume_impl( \ (struct IdealVolumeArgs){ \ .atm=1, .moles=1, .kelvin=273.15, __VA_ARGS__ \ }) double ideal_volume_impl(struct IdealVolumeArgs args) { // The ideal gas law: PV = nRT return args.moles * 0.082057366 * args.kelvin / args.atm; } int main() { printf("1 mole of gas at STP occupies %g L
", ideal_volume()); printf("1 mole of gas at 100°C occupies %g L
", ideal_volume(.kelvin = 373.15)); printf("2 moles of gas at 100°C occupies %g L
", ideal_volume(.kelvin = 373.15, .moles = 2)); printf("2 moles of gas at 0°C and 2 atm occupies %g L
", ideal_volume(.moles = 2, .atm = 2)); } This idiom gives us named, defaultable arguments with natural function-call syntax. It relies on two features of C’s designated initializers that C++20 didn’t adopt: They can appear in any order: (struct IdealVolumeArgs){ .atm=1, .moles=2 } means the same thing as (struct IdealVolumeArgs){ .moles=2, .atm=1 } . The same designator can appear multiple times, and only the last one “sticks”: (struct IdealVolumeArgs){ .atm=1, .moles=2, .atm=3 } means the same thing as (struct IdealVolumeArgs){ .atm=3, .moles=2 } . That second bullet means we’re relying on something that would be bad style if it weren’t intentional. Clang emits a -Winitializer-overrides diagnostic by default. GCC (more sensibly IMHO) emits -Woverride-init only with -Wextra . Once a function uses this idiom, adding a new named parameter to the function definition is no longer an API break! For example, we might decide to let the caller provide their own value for the ideal gas constant R . We simply add a new field to the Args struct. All the old call-sites will still compile just fine, and have the same behavior. (It’s not an API break, but it is an ABI break: the callers needn’t be re- written , but they do need to be re- compiled against the new header.) struct IdealVolumeArgs { double atm; // P double moles; // n double R; // R -- this new field changes ABI double kelvin; // T }; #define ideal_volume(...) ideal_volume_impl((struct IdealVolumeArgs){ \ .atm=1, .moles=1, .R = 0.082057366, .kelvin=273.15, __VA_ARGS__ \ }) double ideal_volume_impl(struct IdealVolumeArgs args) { return args.moles * args.R * args.kelvin / args.atm; } If you’re writing a family of related functions, you can share the Args struct among the whole family; for example, we might add a .liters field to our struct, rename it IdealGasArgs , and define a whole family of functions using that bag of keyword arguments: #define ideal_pressure(...) ideal_pressure_impl((struct IdealGasArgs){ \ .atm=NAN, .moles=1, .kelvin=273.15, .liters=1, __VA

The approach uses de-identified booking sessions and large language models (LLMs) to jointly generate synthetic search queries and relevance labels, enabling model training before sufficient real search traffic is available. By Robert Krzaczyński
articles.summary: Airbnb推出CASTLE框架，利用脱敏预订会话和LLM联合生成合成查询与相关性标签，解决自然语言搜索冷启动问题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #544: AI is now the most-cited risk in the Fed's survey: 87%, up from 50%
articles.content: The Federal Reserve asked its market contacts what could shake the financial system, and 87% named AI, up from 50% in the spring. The same week, the FAA halted flights nationwide days after putting an AI tool in every regional control center, and says it is still looking at what happened. Nvidia's board has approached Arm's CEO about replacing Jensen Huang. Russian pranksters got three OpenAI national security staff on a video call. In the middle: Anthropic prices its IPO on Wednesday with $900.9 billion in compute commitments on its books.
articles.summary: 美联储调查显示87%市场联系人将AI列为最受关注风险，较春季的50%大幅上升，同期FAA因AI工具暂停全国航班。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #543: Google is the latest tech giant to chase TypeSafe's 8-week-old Jev
articles.content: This issue is about decision models, a new kind of AI model that does not write text. You give it an input and a fixed list of answers, and it returns the best answer with a probability, in milliseconds. TypeSafe AI released the first one, Jev, on September 15. On Wednesday Google released its own, after OpenAI and Microsoft did in October, and all three charge $0.10 or less per million input tokens and nothing for output. Shanghai AI Lab says its 4B model beat Jev on its tests, and Microsoft built its model on Alibaba's Qwen. Chatbots still score a little higher on the hardest decisions, at 15 times the cost. In the middle: on Vercel's gateway, decision models took one in four AI requests in October.
articles.summary: TypeSafe AI 发布决策模型 Jev，输入问题与候选答案即毫秒级返回最优解；谷歌本周推出同类产品，加入这一新赛道。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #542: AI week ahead: data center pause backers could win 15 governor races
articles.content: This issue is about the week ahead, and something is scheduled almost every day. On Tuesday, US voters choose 36 governors, and in up to 15 of those races the candidate who backs a pause on new data centers could win. Apple reports earnings today and AMD on Tuesday. On Wednesday, Apple starts testing Apple Intelligence in China with Alibaba's Qwen, and Agility Robotics expects to close its deal to go public. When Congress returns on November 9, OpenAI plans to push for "speed limits" on the most powerful AI. Last week, a fake Claude Code update reached up to 5,000 Cursor users, and in a Cornell and Yale test nine of ten AI models raised their own spending limits. In the middle: insuring Big Tech's debt now costs more than at any time since 2021.
articles.summary: 本周美国36州州长选举中，最多15个支持暂停新建数据中心的候选人有望胜出；苹果、AMD 同日发布财报。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #541: Big Tech reports AI spending Wednesday as CoreWeave debt hits distress
articles.content: This issue looks ahead. On Wednesday the Fed announces its rate decision, then Microsoft and Alphabet report after the close. Amazon follows on Thursday. Investors want to know whether AI spending is still paying off, and the credit market is already nervous: insurance against a CoreWeave default now costs more than 10% a year. Anthropic is expected to file its IPO paperwork publicly any day. Moonshot says Kimi K3.1 Pro's open weights arrive November 4. Israel votes on Tuesday after a campaign full of AI deepfakes, and the US midterms are a week from Tuesday. In the middle: so far, AI has paid off for the companies that sell it, not the ones that buy it.
articles.summary: 微软、Alphabet 周三发布财报，市场关注 AI 投入回报；CoreWeave 债务违约保险成本飙升，信贷市场趋紧。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #540: AI is finding software flaws faster than teams can fix them
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past two weeks, drawn from our Use-Case Library and from SEC filings. Three things stand out: AI now finds security flaws at record volume, AI agents do a large share of the work at some companies, and test agents keep doing things nobody asked them to do.
articles.summary: 企业应用显示 AI 发现安全漏洞的速度已超过团队修复能力，AI 代理承担大量工作，测试代理持续增多。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #539: AI-made midterm ads top $137 million, and 70% carry no AI label
articles.content: Campaigns and PACs have spent more than $137 million on AI-generated or AI-enhanced midterm ads, and about 70% of them carry no AI label, the New York Times reported. The biggest pro-AI super PAC network paid about $20 million to a Nevada company that exists only as a post office box. A new report found 81 of 134 AI models failed a test built from terrorist-style questions. A video game reverse engineering site is closing because AI made the work too easy. Some companies that rushed into AI are now limiting it, and a JAMA study counted 270 million questions doctors asked one AI tool. In the middle: police in Michigan used an AI-generated photo of a teenager to catch a suspect.
articles.summary: 中期选举中 AI 生成或增强广告支出超1.37亿美元，约70%未标注 AI；某超级 PAC 向空壳公司支付约2000万美元。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #537: AI models may soon copy themselves onto smart fridges, Anthropic says
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared most since our last issue on October 8, minus the stories we already sent you in the Daily Espresso. The most shared: Anthropic's warning that small AI models may soon be able to copy themselves onto home devices. Also: a large study of what AI coding agents change at real companies, a fight over how to check AI math proofs, creative workers pushing back on AI, and police buying more AI.
articles.summary: Anthropic 警告小型 AI 模型或将能自我复制到智能冰箱等家用设备，引发对 AI 扩散风险的关注。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #536: Top AI models failed a test of inventing new AI research
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared over the past three days. Most of them look ahead: whether AI can do AI research on its own, who gets a say in governing it, how it is moving into war planning, and how it is moving onto personal computers.
articles.summary: 顶尖 AI 模型在自主开展 AI 研究的测试中失败；专家关注 AI 治理话语权、军事规划应用及 PC 端落地。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #535: AI got too expensive, so companies are moving to cheaper models
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past three weeks. Three patterns stand out: companies switching models to control cost, large deployments that are now in daily use, and a growing list of places where AI was restricted or removed.
articles.summary: AI 成本过高促使企业转向更便宜的模型，大规模部署进入日常使用，同时越来越多场景开始限制或移除 AI。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #534: Universities cannot grade their way out of AI
articles.content: This week, campus IT leaders voted AI their top priority for the first time, Cambridge refused Turnitin's new terms over AI training on student work, Dartmouth opened an investigation into its own provost's writing, and Ken Griffin gave Carnegie Mellon $3 billion. Student AI use is no longer a future scenario. The useful question for universities is whether they can teach students to work with AI and still certify what those students can do without it. New evidence from tutoring trials, assessment redesigns, student-support systems and campus data deals points to a practical answer.
articles.summary: 高校 IT 负责人首次将 AI 列为首要任务；剑桥拒绝 Turnitin 新条款，达特茅斯调查教务长写作，AI 使用已非未来议题。

articles.title: All your packages are belong to us
articles.content: AI agents can write the code, choose the packages, and run the install. Who's checking what they just invited onto your machine? This week I'm joined by Ahmad Nassri, CTO of Socket and former CTO of npm. We get into the trust built into a package install, the new ways attackers are using agents, and what it takes to keep building without handing over the keys or your wallet.
articles.summary: Socket CTO 谈 AI 代理自动选包安装带来的供应链风险，以及攻击者利用代理的新手法与包安装信任机制。

articles.title: We now have Kerr’s Law
articles.content: Dave Kerr created hacker laws, and now he finds himself reviewing agent-written code for them. Back on the show after six years, Dave names what he sees limiting teams today: keeping everyone’s mental model in sync with what’s actually been built. Adam declares it Kerr’s Law on the spot. We get into why Dave’s team treats code review as a deliberate slowdown, how Shellwright lets agents bring evidence to a pull request, and what living with bipolar disorder has taught Dave about noticing when the excitement of these tools stops being healthy.
articles.summary: Dave Kerr 提出“Kerr 定律”：团队最大瓶颈是让所有人的心智模型与实际构建成果保持同步。

articles.title: The future is Postgres
articles.content: Craig Kerstiens returns to talk about the ever-expanding world of Postgres: a deliberately boring core, a thriving extension ecosystem, and pg_lake bringing DuckDB and Iceberg into the mix. We dig into the pain of ETL, what Craig is watching in Postgres 19, the impact of AI on open source maintainers, and why the database still has plenty of room to grow.
articles.summary: Craig Kerstiens 谈 Postgres 扩展生态与 pg_lake 引入 DuckDB、Iceberg，以及 AI 对开源维护者的影响。

articles.title: Building what's next
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Zeno Rocha, CEO of Resend, about scaling "boring" email to 3 million users, the secret Go rewrite behind it, and building for agents. We cover pricing.md, MCP, spam gangs, and why Resend keeps what's next for email.
articles.summary: Resend CEO Zeno Rocha 分享用 Go 重写支撑300万用户的邮件服务，并探讨面向 AI 代理的产品设计与定价。

articles.title: From zero to NanoClaw
articles.content: Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project's community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private. They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw's "skills over features" approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam's case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.
articles.summary: Gavriel Cohen 讲述周末40小时项目 NanoClaw 如何成为爆款开源项目，并发展为容器隔离的企业级 AI 公司。

articles.title: Forking Cal.com to closed source
articles.content: This week I'm joined by Peer Richelsen, co-founder of Cal.com. What if the majority of open source repositories are already compromised and we just don't know it yet? That's the theory Peer brings to the table this week. We dig into how AI has flattened the knowledge graph to the point that a 16-year-old can vibe hack a power station just as easily as their mom can vibe code an iOS app, why the reporting culture that has kept open source safe all these years is collapsing under AI generated noise, Cal.com's move to fork its own codebase and take the sensitive parts private, and the eye opening reality that shipping "$1 of AI tokens for pennies on the dollar" is now a common startup business model.
articles.summary: Cal.com 联合创始人 Peer Richelsen 提出多数开源仓库可能已被攻陷的猜想，并讨论 AI 对知识门槛的冲击。

articles.title: Postgres at PlanetScale
articles.content: Sam Lambert is back after 4 years and he does not hold back! We cover $5 PlanetScale Postgres, the Neki "do-over" of Vitess, agents shipping schema changes through deploy requests, rolling back a 500TB table in seconds, and the very real question of whether to open source any of it. Plus: why he thinks the sleeping, lazy giants should be broken up.
articles.summary: PlanetScale CEO 谈5美元 Postgres 方案、Vitess 重做、代理提交 schema 变更及500TB 表秒级回滚。

articles.title: Canary tokens and digital tripwires
articles.content: Haroon Meer is back! Haroon is the Founder of Thinkst, the ~50-person bootstrapped company behind Canary and Canarytokens — honeypots and tripwires you sprinkle inside your network and forget about until an attacker touches one. We talk about the AWS API key token attackers just can't resist trying, the real credit card token backed by an actual bank partnership, Breadcrumbs (their brand-new feature that leads intruders straight to your canaries), a live demo where a hardware Canary becomes a Synology NAS in one click, and how a company with zero outbound sales and no price increase in ten years quietly passed $22.5 million in ARR.
articles.summary: Thinkst 创始人 Haroon Meer 介绍 Canary 与 Canarytokens 蜜罐诱饵工具，可部署于网络内静默监测攻击者触碰行为。

articles.title: From open source hits to OpenAI
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Max Stoiber, currently working on ChatGPT's plugin directory and app platform at OpenAI. We discuss the hundreds of open source projects nobody remembers alongside the big ones like react-boilerplate and styled-components, how Spectrum became part of GitHub and eventually helped shape GitHub Discussions, the founder growth that came from building Stellate, the GraphQL cache that turned into a dual acquisition by Shopify and The Guild, and why ChatGPT apps feel like a new surface for software.
articles.summary: Max Stoiber 讲述从 react-boilerplate 等开源项目到加入 OpenAI 负责 ChatGPT 插件目录与平台开发的经历。

articles.title: US Officially a Measles Endemic Country
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Hill: The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) confirmed Tuesday that it was withdrawing the U.S.'s measles elimination status, ending more than two decades of what is considered to be one of the greatest public health achievements in modern history. The U.S. met with PAHO's Measles and Rubella Elimination Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission for a three-day, closed-door meeting last week. "The commission concluded that the endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn, a recommendation which I have accepted," Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO's director, said during the briefing Tuesday. The U.S. achieved measles elimination status in 2000 and has held onto that for more than 25 years. But the past two years have seen close to 8,000 measles infections and roughly a dozen related deaths. This year has been the worst in terms of transmission in more than 30 years. Erica Schwartz, director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has previously said losing elimination status won't lead to changes in the federal response. "We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities," Schwartz said on Tuesday. "Losing a designation doesn't mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks." Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 泛美卫生组织撤销美国麻疹消除状态，结束二十余年公共卫生成就，美国正式成为麻疹地方性流行国家。

articles.title: Nvidia Rejects Jensen Huang's Offer to Return as CEO
articles.content: Nvidia's board has unanimously rejected former CEO Jensen Huang's offer to return, despite public support from President Trump and prominent Silicon Valley figures. The decision came as Nvidia reported blockbuster third-quarter revenue of $116 billion, double the year-earlier figure. The Associated Press reports: The embattled company's board of directors "unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said at the start of Nvidia's quarterly earnings call before yielding to Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, who is running the company as a permanent replacement is sought. [...] Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said in a social media post that if the board decided that his return was in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company and the country, he would be "honored to answer these calls." He acknowledged making "serious mistakes" in his personal life. The turmoil notwithstanding, Nvidia blew past Wall Street expectations for the third quarter, pulling in $116 billion in revenue, double the level from a year ago. The company also posted net income of $2.70 per share, beating estimates of $2.48 per share. Nvidia stock shot up 5.2% in after-hours trading. Referring to Huang's replacement, Jones said, "We want to install the permanent CEO as quickly as possible, but we won't expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person." Nvidia also announced a new board committee overseeing national security and trade compliance amid investigations into alleged AI chip smuggling to China. Further reading: Nvidia Stopped Disclosing Singapore Sales As Revenues Hit $104 Billion Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 英伟达董事会一致拒绝前 CEO 黄仁勋回归提议，同期公司公布第三季度 1160 亿美元营收，同比翻倍。

articles.title: Google To Keep Temporary Gemini Chats For Two Months
articles.content: timob58 shares a report from TechCrunch: Google is extending how long it keeps temporary Gemini chats and conversations made with chat history turned off to around two months, saying the change aims to improve safety and security as AI systems become more capable. The change, which will roll out globally in the Gemini app over the coming weeks, marks a significant increase from the previous 72-hour retention period mentioned in Google's Gemini Apps Privacy Hub, according to an archived version from November 12. OpenAI, by comparison, says it may keep temporary chats in ChatGPT for up to 30 days, whereas Anthropic retains incognito chats in Claude for 30 days by default. Google did not answer questions about what prompted the change and whether it would affect how conversations are accessed or reviewed, instead pointing to a blog post that says chats are kept longer to respond to users, process feedback, and protect its services and users. Its updated Gemini Apps Privacy Hub also cites potential system failures as a reason for retaining chats and says temporary conversations are not used to train AI models. "A recent explainer on AI and business IP notes that providers keep data for abuse monitoring even when it is not used for training," adds timob58. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 谷歌将 Gemini 临时对话及关闭历史记录对话的保留期延长至约两个月，称旨在提升 AI 系统安全。

articles.title: Optimizely Hack Turns World's Biggest Websites Into Malware Dispensers
articles.content: PattonPending writes: As reported by The Register, Zoom, the BBC, CNN, HSBC, and numerous other websites briefly served malware on November 16 after an attacker exploited Optimizely's "Experiments" feature to inject JavaScript into their pages through Optimizely's CDN. The malware replaced cryptocurrency addresses, attempted to steal credit card information and cookies, and sought to compromise iOS devices. Websites belonging to at least 178 organizations were affected via the "OPTIMJACK" vulnerability, which has since been patched. "Earlier today, Optimizely identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects," the company said. "We've fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects. We've also taken steps to secure affected user accounts and put additional protections in place to prevent unauthorized code from being delivered." The researchers said they found malicious code in 188 of the 1,611 Optimizely scripts examined, including those on the company's own website and login portal, suggesting the number of affected businesses could be significantly higher. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 攻击者利用 Optimizely 实验功能注入 JavaScript，致 Zoom、BBC、CNN 等网站短暂投放恶意软件。

articles.title: School Phone Bans Are Gradually Improving Test Scores
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from The New York Times: School cellphone bans are beginning to modestly improve students' academic performance, according to the first large national analysis that compared students' test scores before and after the bans. Schools with strict bans -- requiring students to lock their phones in pouches all school day -- saw math and reading scores improve as if students had an additional week or two of school a year, the study found. It was published Tuesday by the Center for Education Policy Research at Harvard. U.S. students' test scores began falling over a decade ago. The drop coincided with the rise of smartphones, raising questions about their role in the decline. The evidence so far on the academic effects of phone bans has been mixed. But the new study indicates they are starting to have an influence. The study looked at 3.3 million students between 2021 and 2026. They were in third through 10th grade, attending 4,600 U.S. schools. Using scores on MAP tests, which track achievement from fall to spring, it compared the performance of students at schools that put in strict phone bans with those at similar schools that did not have such bans. The annual gains reversed about half the annual loss that an average student experienced in the years leading up to the pandemic. (Students lost even more ground during pandemic closures.) "The earlier studies on cellphone bans have been dismissed as implying small impacts, and in-school cellphone use has been ruled out as playing a big role in the decline," said Thomas Kane, a professor at the Harvard Graduate School of Education and an author of the study. "But we think that's mistaken." Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 首项全国性大规模分析显示，学校严格手机禁令开始小幅提升学生考试成绩。

articles.title: BugMeNot Calls It Quits
articles.content: BugMeNot, the password-sharing service launched in 2003 to help users bypass website registration requirements, has shut down without explanation after more than two decades. All that's left on the website is a farewell message that reads: "Thanks to everyone who envisioned a better internet." heise online reports: Founded by Guy King, the service had been online since 2003: BugMeNot was a collection of login credentials for various online services. Volunteers submitted credentials they had created for different websites. The idea was simple: Nobody wants to create a full account and provide all their sensitive information just to use a service occasionally. Two decades ago, this privacy concern was more firmly embedded in the public consciousness, but it has since faded considerably. Back then, usernames and passwords were usually the only access controls, so people could easily submit those credentials. Multifactor authentication was still exotic, and passkeys were a distant prospect. The once-popular service lost its shine after just a few years. Service providers quickly discovered and blocked most of the credentials. They could also prevent users from saving logins for their services directly through BugMeNot, for example when those services were paid. More modern security mechanisms also emerged in recent years. As a result, credentials found on BugMeNot rarely worked. Most online providers also blocked the service's disposable email addresses under @bugmenot.com, making them rarely usable. Many people forgot about the site. Now its operators have shut it down without giving a reason. Additional discussions about BugMeNot's closure can be found on Reddit and Hacker News. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 运行二十余年的密码共享服务 BugMeNot 无预警关停，网站仅留告别信息。

articles.title: Uber Says Hackers Stole Info On Nearly 150K Driver's Licenses During Data Breach
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from TechCrunch: Uber is notifying close to 150,000 drivers that their personal and driver's license information was stolen during an October data breach at one of the company's tech providers. In notices filed this week with several U.S. attorneys general, including California and Iowa, the ride-hailing giant said it was notified on October 9 by the provider that hackers broke in and stole internal credentials, which were used to access Uber's data. The company said it subsequently began notifying affected drivers that their personal information was stored with the provider. The stolen data includes affected drivers' names, addresses, dates of birth, and driver's license numbers. TechCrunch has learned that the provider is Fireworks AI, which lets developers access and use open-weight AI models. Fireworks reported a data breach last month in which hackers stole its customers' information, including billing data and some private AI datasets. Online productivity startup Notion and AI coding startup Cursor have both confirmed that they had data stolen during the Fireworks hack. In Uber's case, the company said it had alerts enabled to detect unauthorized access to its Fireworks environment, but because the hackers used Fireworks' own internal credentials, "no alerts were triggered." [...] In a notice filed with Oregon's attorney general, Uber said it notified 149,346 people in total that their information had been taken in the breach at Fireworks. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: Uber 通报十月第三方供应商数据泄露事件，近 15 万名司机的个人信息和驾照信息被盗。

articles.title: JavaScript Geometry Orthogonalize library
articles.content: JavaScript Geometry Orthogonalize library Squares the corners of GeoJSON lines and polygons (e.g. building footprints), so that every segment becomes horizontal or vertical on an orthogonal grid, aligned either to the cardinal directions or to the dominant orientation of the shape. Orthogonalize(options, geojson) accepts any GeoJSON object (Geometry, Feature or FeatureCollection) containing LineString/Polygon geometries and returns a new orthogonalized GeoJSON; the input is not modified. Options: const OrthoOpts = { orientationMode : "cardinal" // align to north/south/east/west (default) //orientationMode: "original" // keep the dominant orientation of the shape } ; const fs = require ( 'fs' ) ; const Orthogonalize = require ( 'orthogonalize-js' ) ; const geojson = JSON . parse ( fs . readFileSync ( 'examples/shape.json' , 'utf8' ) ) ; const geojsonOrto = Orthogonalize ( { orientationMode : "cardinal" } , geojson ) ; fs . writeFileSync ( 'shape_ortho.json' , JSON . stringify ( geojsonOrto , null , 2 ) ) ; < script src =" https://unpkg.com/orthogonalize-js/orthogonalize.src.js " > </ script > var map = L . map ( 'map' , { zoom : 17 , center : [ 42.31981 , 12.69832 ] , layers : L . tileLayer ( 'https://{s}.tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png' ) } ) ; var geoLayer = L . geoJson ( null , { style : { color : '#0000ff' , weight : 5 } } ) . addTo ( map ) ; var geoOrto = L . geoJson ( null , { style : { color : '#ff0000' , weight : 2 } } ) . addTo ( map ) ; fetch ( 'shape.json' ) . then ( res => res . json ( ) ) . then ( geojson => { geoLayer . addData ( geojson ) ; geoOrto . addData ( Orthogonalize ( OrthoOpts , geojson ) ) ; map . fitBounds ( geoLayer . getBounds ( ) ) ; } ) ; See the full demos in examples/

articles.title: Sometimes three boring statements beats one clever expression
articles.content: Modern JavaScript gives us a lot of expressive tools. Sometimes a little too many. Optional chaining, nullish coalescing, ternaries, spread, template literals. I like all of them and use them every day. But together, they make it really easy to cram a lot of logic into a single expression. I used to think that was a sign of good JavaScript. I’m not so sure anymore. When one more ?? is too many Take something like this: const theme = config?.theme ?? user?.preferences?.theme ?? defaults.theme; I’ve written this plenty of times. It’s short and it works. But once these expressions start growing, they read more like puzzles than code: const theme = config?.theme ?? user?.preferences?.theme ?? getFallbackTheme() ?? defaults.theme; I can follow it, but I have to stop and parse it. Compare that to this: let theme = config?.theme; if (theme == null) { theme = user?.preferences?.theme; } if (theme == null) { theme = getFallbackTheme(); } return theme ?? defaults.theme; More lines? Sure. But it’s a lot more obvious. Yes, I give up const and reassign a variable. I’ll take that trade. Long expressions hide decisions Longer expressions squeeze several decisions into one piece of syntax. The more you chain, the more you have to work out at once: What happens if config is undefined? Where does the fallback come from? Which value wins? What if getFallbackTheme() throws? Chaining saves some vertical space, but you have to hold more in your head. It’s a practical problem, too. You can’t put a breakpoint on one fallback in the middle of a ?? chain, and you can’t log a single step without rewriting the expression. With separate statements, every step gets its own line to stop on or log. The diffs are nicer, as well. Adding a fallback means adding a block, not editing one dense line. Plain statements are fine A lot of us started treating plain if statements as something to avoid. So we’d rather write this: return user?.isAdmin ? getDashboard(user) : getLandingPage(user); than this: if (user?.isAdmin) { return getDashboard(user); } return getLandingPage(user); Neither one is objectively better. The second isn’t “less modern,” it’s often just easier to read. A single ternary like that is fine. It’s when they nest that I stop: return isLoading ? "Loading" : error ? "Failed to load" : items.length === 0 ? "Nothing here yet" : `${items.length} items`; The same thing with plain statements: if (isLoading) return "Loading"; if (error) return "Failed to load"; if (items.length === 0) return "Nothing here yet"; return `${items.length} items`; Clever code gets old fast Over the past couple of years I’ve found myself chaining less and writing fewer nested ternaries. I don’t mind adding another if anymore. I care more about readability than being clever. When I’m debugging production code or reviewing a pull request, I can’t remember ever wishing something had been written as one bigger expression. My rule of thumb is simple. A chain of plain values is fine. Once there’s a functi

articles.title: Xec - TypeScript automation for local, SSH, Docker, and Kubernetes workflows (v0.13)
articles.content: TYPESCRIPT AUTOMATION, WITHOUT THE SEAMS v0.13 Make the work flow. Your scripts. Your CLI. Every environment. Turn the work around your code into clear, reusable TypeScript. From a local command to a release pipeline, keep execution, credentials and data under your control. Security and privacy are part of the execution contract. Read the guarantees and current scope. $ npm install -g @xec-sh/cli → ❯ One toolkit. Your environment. TYPESCRIPT inspect.ts Copy import { $ } from '@xec-sh/core' ; const revision = await $ `git rev-parse --short HEAD` . timeout ( '10s' ) . text (); console. log (revision. trim ()); Run in a Git repository with xec run inspect.ts. Commands use the selected local shell. Read the guide → ONE EXECUTION CONTRACT Local / SSH / Docker / Kubernetes Node.js · Bun · Deno libraries 01 / FROM ONE COMMAND TO A SYSTEM Start small. Keep the same foundations. Adopt the library, the CLI, or both. Each layer has one job and works with the tools you already use. 02 / COMPOSE, DON'T REWRITE A small surface. A complete execution path. Xec orchestrates the work. Your compiler builds it, Turbo can manage the package graph, and your platform supervises the deployed applications. Explore the architecture 03 / CONTROL IS THE FEATURE Less glue. More intent. 01 Typed where it matters. Compose commands and inspect typed results. Treat shell source and external output as runtime boundaries, not compile-time guarantees. Write portable scripts → 02 Failures stay visible. Choose deadlines, cancellation and retry policies explicitly. Define rollback for your system; an execution library cannot invent it. Handle failure → 03 Tools stay composable. Run locally, from any CI provider, or against your own infrastructure. Keep build caches, credentials and deployment policy under your control. Build a workflow → THE NEXT USEFUL COMMAND Make it yours. One script is enough to get started. Write your first script

articles.title: pathmask matches relative paths against patterns in the syntax of .gitignore
articles.content: Match paths using .gitignore syntax. Use pathmask to filter files by including or excluding matching paths. Requires Node.js 20 or newer. ESM only. Create a mask from patterns and test each path with matches() . import { PathMask } from 'pathmask' ; const mask = new PathMask ( [ 'src/**/*.js' , 'docs/' , '*.md' , '!CHANGELOG.md' , ] ) ; mask . matches ( 'src/index.js' ) ; // true mask . matches ( 'src/cli/run.js' ) ; // true mask . matches ( 'test/index.js' ) ; // false mask . matches ( 'docs/logo.png' ) ; // true mask . matches ( 'local/logo.png' ) ; // false mask . matches ( 'README.md' ) ; // true mask . matches ( 'test/README.md' ) ; // true mask . matches ( 'CHANGELOG.md' ) ; // false Tools often get a list of paths from a config and need to filter it, for example to choose which files to build, lint or deploy. The .gitignore syntax is the format every developer already knows for such rules. It is based on the basic POSIX glob syntax with * , ? and [...] , and adds a few simple rules for lists of paths. pathmask tests a given path against these rules and follows the behavior of git, so a pattern means the same here and in .gitignore . Short rules: a pattern without / matches at any depth, dist/ matches a directory with all its contents. Exceptions: patterns are applied in order, ! brings a path back. Dotfiles: * matches names that start with . , no options needed. One reference: git defines the behavior, there are no library-specific options. For common rules, the .gitignore syntax is shorter and easier to read than glob. glob pathmask ['**/node_modules/**', '**/*.log'] ['node_modules/', '*.log'] ['**/*.log', '!**/keep.log'] ['*.log', '!keep.log'] ['**/dist', '**/dist/**'] ['dist/'] ['**/.*'] with the option { dot: true } ['.*'] To write glob patterns with {a,b} and extglob in pathmask, see Glob equivalents . Creates a path matcher from an array of patterns in .gitignore syntax. Parameter Type Description patterns string[] Patterns in .gitignore syntax, see Patterns . Throws a TypeError when patterns is not an array of strings, see Errors . Tests a relative path against the patterns. Parameter Type Description path string A path relative to the root, see Paths . Returns true if the mask matches the path or a directory that contains it. Otherwise, returns false . Throws a TypeError when the path is invalid, see Errors . Keep the paths that the mask does not match. Create the mask once and reuse it for all paths. const excluded = new PathMask ( [ 'node_modules/' , '*.log' , '.*' ] ) ; const paths = [ 'README.md' , 'debug.log' , '.env' , 'src/index.js' , 'node_modules/ansis/index.js' ] ; const files = paths . filter ( ( file ) => ! excluded . matches ( file ) ) ; // ['README.md', 'src/index.js'] Exclude files in a directory Read the files of my-project and keep the files that the mask does not match. import { readdirSync , statSync } from 'node:fs' ; import path from 'node:path' ; import { PathMask } from 'pathmask' ; const rootPath = './my-pro

articles.title: Announcing Parcel 3 Alpha
articles.content: Announcing Parcel 3 alpha 2026-11-04 Today we're releasing the first alpha of Parcel 3, a ground up rewrite of Parcel in Rust. It is up to 100x faster than v2, and supports native plugins written in Rust, Go, Swift, or C, as well as a custom runtime for JavaScript and TypeScript plugins. It also includes improved automatic code splitting, library mode, tree shaking, centralized configuration, and much more. Why a rewrite? In Parcel v2, we rewrote several individual pieces of Parcel in Rust. First was our JavaScript compiler , built on top of SWC. Then, we built Lightning CSS . Later, we rebuilt our HTML and SVG transformer and optimizers. However, Parcel's core was still written in JavaScript. This limited our maximum possible performance due to lack of shared memory between threads, high memory usage, garbage collection, and the cost of serializing values between workers and languages. Parcel v3 is an entirely self-contained Rust binary, with no dependency on Node at all. Everything from the CLI and dev server, to the transformers, bundler, optimizers, and everything in between is now fully native. This enables us to efficiently take full advantage of modern multi-core hardware. The results speak for themselves: up to 100x faster builds using the same underlying compilers as v2, only changing the core. Performance Let's cut to the benchmarks. Here's a comparison of cold development builds between v2 and v3 for React Spectrum , a large TypeScript monorepo. For reference: Storybook : ~100 entries, JS macros , custom plugins ported to Rust for Parcel 3. Docs website : ~340 pages, React Server Components, MDX, Tailwind, custom plugins. Library build : ~160 packages, TSX, macros, CSS modules, SVG icons. Outputs over 14,000 files. Development build time Cold development build time, Parcel 2 vs Parcel 3 Storybook: Parcel 2 16.62s, Parcel 3 572ms (29× faster). Docs website: Parcel 2 87.59s, Parcel 3 810ms (108× faster). Library build: Parcel 2 131.47s, Parcel 3 2.71s (49× faster). Storybook Storybook – Parcel 2: 16.62s 16.62s Storybook – Parcel 3: 572ms (29× faster) 572ms · 29× faster Docs website Docs website – Parcel 2: 87.59s 87.59s Docs website – Parcel 3: 810ms (108× faster) 810ms · 108× faster Library build Library build – Parcel 2: 131.47s 131.47s Library build – Parcel 3: 2.71s (49× faster) 2.71s · 49× faster Parcel 2 Parcel 3 Memory usage Memory usage, Parcel 2 vs Parcel 3 Storybook: Parcel 2 7.7GB, Parcel 3 1.5GB (5.1× less). Docs website: Parcel 2 13.9GB, Parcel 3 2.1GB (6.6× less). Library build: Parcel 2 5.7GB, Parcel 3 2.3GB (2.5× less). Storybook Storybook – Parcel 2: 7.7GB 7.7GB Storybook – Parcel 3: 1.5GB (5.1× less) 1.5GB · 5.1× less Docs website Docs website – Parcel 2: 13.9GB 13.9GB Docs website – Parcel 3: 2.1GB (6.6× less) 2.1GB · 6.6× less Library build Library build – Parcel 2: 5.7GB 5.7GB Library build – Parcel 3: 2.3GB (2.5× less) 2.3GB · 2.5× less Parcel 2 Parcel 3 Speed without caching In Parcel 2, we heavily invested in disk

articles.title: Goyangi: watch what Claude Code is doing, live: every step, tool call, subagent, token and cost in a side panel
articles.content: Goyangi is a panel beside your Claude Code conversation that shows, turn by turn, where the time and money went. Goyangi (고양이) is the Korean word for a cat: a cat that sits next to the conversation and watches every turn. claude plugin marketplace add netil/goyangi claude plugin install goyangi@goyangi --scope user Run /reload-plugins , then open the panel with /goyangi . It also opens by itself when a session starts. New versions install automatically (turn this off in the settings screen, = in the header). Sessions and browser tabs have numbers, so a short prompt is enough: send this to session 2 pull from 1 Summarize the docs tab Work in tab B3 send this to session 2 passes this session's handoff note to the other session. pull from 1 asks session 1 for its handoff Summarize the docs tab and Work in tab B3 work in that very browser tab, with your sign-ins. The numbers come from the Open sessions and Browser tabs boxes When context passes the alert threshold, click Continue in a fresh session and the work carries on in a new session from a handoff note Turn flow : every model request, tool call, and subagent of the turn in order, with tokens, cost, and a time share bar Gauges and advice : context, cache hit rate, and the 5h and 7d usage limits with a forecast. Rule-based advice flags repeated failures, cache drops, and files read again. All computed locally, no tokens spent Session map and log : one row per turn to compare, and a replay of any recent turn. The log switches between key events and everything Walk and compact views : press v and a pixel cat or dog walks through the turn, its mood showing context, cost, and usage limits. Press again for a compact two-row track of the steps Forks : start a prompt with ; and it runs in a background session in its own git worktree while you keep working here. Its permission requests come to this panel, and it merges back when its tests pass Fresh session : past a token point (200k by default), the work moves to a new session in the same window with a handoff note instead of compacting Open sessions : send this session's handoff to another Claude Code session or a coding agent (Codex, OpenCode, ...), or pull theirs here Browser tabs : your open tabs, numbered. Say "B3" or "the GitHub PR tab" and the model works in that tab Terminal and desktop app : the same panel in both The walk view's cat and dog: running, thinking, working, failing, and sleeping. See the manual for the layout, shortcuts, advice rules, and settings . Claude Code with mod (function hooks) support The walk view's pixel art uses octant characters (Unicode 16) in Ghostty, kitty, and WezTerm. Other terminals (Obsidian's terminal, iTerm2, Terminal.app, VS Code) get a coarser version drawn with quadrant blocks, so the layout holds claude plugin validate . claude plugin test . articles.title: We Migrated 10,144 Tests from Jest to Vitest in 3 Weeks: The Honest, AI-Assisted Truth
articles.content: A note on the Vitest version: This migration was carried out in August 2026, using Vitest 4 . All the figures, benchmarks, configuration details, and lessons described in this article refer to Vitest 4, not Vitest 5. Migrating a test runner is rarely a magic "swap and go" operation. Our experience moving our entire frontend test suite from Jest to Vitest was a real engineering undertaking, filled with bottlenecks, meticulous pool tuning, unmasked bugs, one rollback, and one optimization we shipped and then had to take back. Over the course of about three weeks, our frontend team migrated eight repositories. We didn't settle for file counts; we ran every suite end-to-end to get the real numbers. Here is the exact scale of what we achieved: 10,144 executed unit tests, real numbers from actually running the suites, not file counts. 1,799 test files across 8 repositories. 0 repos left in a half-migrated state. ~3 weeks to complete the entire effort, migrations plus the tuning that followed. ~$751 estimated AI token cost for the Claude Code sessions we could trace to this work. See the caveats on that number below: it's a rough upper bound, not a bill. This is the story of what actually happened, drawn directly from our git history, PR bodies, and session logs, to help you navigate your own migration. To save you some of the pain we went through, we also published a generalized version of the AI automation skill we ended up wishing we'd had from day one: github.com/Subito-it/articles-code/tree/main/jest-to-vitest-migration . Why Jest started hurting We didn't decide to migrate just because "Jest is slow" in the abstract. We migrated because maintaining it had become an active, recurring tax on our engineering time. We also wanted to be on the side of where the ecosystem was heading, since Vitest was fast becoming the default choice for new Vite/Next.js projects. 1. The CommonJS vs. ESM nightmare By default, next/jest skips transforming anything inside node_modules , so when a dependency ships an ESM-only update, Jest's CommonJS require() fails. We found ourselves hand-patching transformIgnorePatterns regexes to allow-list specific packages. Here's the exact code comment from our config, verbatim: // ESM-only node_modules that Jest must transform. next/jest overwrites any // user-supplied transformIgnorePatterns to skip all of node_modules, so we // allow-list these on the resolved config instead. const esmPackagesToTransform = [ ' cookie ' ]; Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Separately, and about six weeks before we'd even decided to migrate: a major version bump of uuid shipped as pure ESM and broke Jest outright. The real commit message: "uuid v14 ships as pure ESM which breaks Jest (CommonJS). Replace the single usage of uuid() ... with the native crypto.randomUUID() ... removing the dependency entirely." Rather than fight the transform config again, the team just deleted the dependency. When your test runner is dictating your dependency

articles.title: Repo-Atlas - Any GitHub user’s work, mapped and clustered, with stale favorites flagged.
articles.content: Type a GitHub username, get the map of what they've actually built: repos clustered by topic, the highlight of each group, and stars over time. Live: https://evoluteur.github.io/repo-atlas/ · permalink per user: ?u=<username> The map. Every public repo as a disc (area ∝ stars), grouped into regions of repos that share topics. Hover for details, click to open the repo. Groups by stars. The legend ranks the regions by the stars they hold, so you see where the attention actually sits. Highlights. The most-starred repo in each group as a card, with its description, language and live-demo link. Hover a card to find its group on the map; the share card lists the top three. Stars over time. Without a token: stars held today, stacked by the year each repo was born. With a token: real cumulative star history per group, from stargazer dates. Share. A 1200×630 card for social posts and a permalink. Each repo's topics are normalised (plurals folded, generic tags like javascript , svg , ui dropped) and hyphenated topics also contribute their parts ( sacred-geometry → sacred , geometry ). Tokens are weighted by inverse document frequency across the account. Tokens used once, or by more than 45% of repos, carry no signal and are dropped. Repos with almost no topics fall back to description words. Repos are compared by cosine similarity and merged bottom-up (average linkage) until no two groups are more than 0.16 alike. The eight groups holding the most stars get a color and a two-word name (the tokens most frequent inside the group and rarest outside it). Everything else folds into loners . All of this is in src/atlas.js : pure functions, no DOM, tested with node --test . Everything runs in the browser against the public GitHub REST API. The map and the highlights work anonymously (60 requests/hour per IP; a typical account takes 2). GitHub only lists when each star was given to authenticated callers, so the star-history chart needs a token. A fine-grained token with no extra permissions is enough. It is kept in sessionStorage for the tab and only sent to api.github.com . Big repos are sampled: every stargazer page for repos under 500 stars, otherwise the first, last and three evenly spaced pages. Each fetched star is an exact (count, date) point; months in between are interpolated. Results are cached in localStorage (repos 1 hour, star history 24 hours). If the API can't be reached (rate limit, offline), the page lets you paste the JSON from api.github.com/users/<login>/repos?per_page=100 and maps that instead. No build step. Serve the folder and open it: npx serve . # or: python3 -m http.server open http://localhost:3000/ ? u=evoluteur npm test # clustering, highlights and timeline math npm run build # dist/repo-atlas.html: one self-contained file index.html page shell src/atlas.js clustering, highlights, timelines (pure, Node-testable) src/github.js REST client: repos, sampled stargazer pages src/charts.js D3: circle-pack map, birth-year columns, stacked sta
